19995-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for February 1860 is volume 5, number 28. One essay here ponders ancient counting systems. Counting by five fingers and two hands produced the numbers, it argues. Multiplication by five and by two alternately explains the pattern. The Romans adhered to their own mode through it all. Such learned miscellany filled the young magazine's pages. The Atlantic was then barely three years old.

Boston's magazine was already America's literary flagship by 1860. Emerson, Longfellow, and Holmes stood among its founders' circle. Fiction, poetry, science, and review shared each number. February 1860 sits on the edge of a nation about to split. Its calm learning is itself poignant evidence. The issue preserves prewar American intellect at ease.
20033-quin:
Quin appeared in 1921, a novel that opens in the world of dance and wounded men. One man has lain on his back for six months. His legs are still too shaky to hold him well. A friend asks, in sharp words, why he wants to go to a dance at all.

That clash sets the tone for a story about pride, loss, and the wish to live fully again. Talk runs fierce and plain between the men. Readers meet a lead figure who refuses to accept a smaller life. The dance floor becomes a test of will.
20088-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-16-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for November 1865 gathers essays, tales, and verse from leading writers. Volume sixteen, number ninety-seven, came just months after the Civil War ended. One piece weighs beliefs about death across many peoples and faiths. It names Charon and his boat, Dante, and the Muslim hope of paradise.

Monthly issues like this one shaped American thought in the 1860s. Readers of the day found new poems beside grave essays on faith. The issue shows a nation turning from war to deep questions again. It still serves as a window on postwar American letters and belief.
20195-wood-block-printing-a-description-:
F. Morley Fletcher wrote Wood Block Printing, a craft guide based on Japanese practice. Fletcher laments that design was long treated as mere surface looks. Ornament was copied in a mechanical way from an artist's drawing. That artist often knew little of how the work was truly made.

Japanese woodcut craft joins design and making in one skilled hand. Fletcher teaches cutting, inking, and printing step by step for artists. His book helped revive fine woodblock work in the West. Readers get clear craft teaching rooted in respect for the maker's hand.
20203-autobiography-of-benjamin-franklin:
Benjamin Franklin wrote his Autobiography, one of the most read American life stories. This 1916 edition opens with Thomas Jefferson's tale of Franklin at court. Franklin played chess with the old Duchess of Bourbon in France. When he took her king, she said kings are not taken so.

We do in America, Franklin replied, in Jefferson's fond retelling. Inside, Franklin tells of his rise from printer's boy to famed statesman. He shares his plan for moral growth and his shrewd worldly wit. Readers get the classic American tale of self-making, told by its hero.
20232-three-score-years-and-ten-life-lon:
Three Score Years and Ten holds life-long memories of Fort Snelling and the West. One scene recalls a Hartford sitting-room when the century was nineteen. A fair young matron sat beside a cradle in that bright room. In it slept a beautiful boy of a year and a half.

From that tender start, a long life runs west to frontier posts. Fort Snelling stood where rivers meet, at the edge of settlement. Memory books like this one save daily life that histories skip. Readers get seventy years of family, army, and western change in one voice.
20430-the-after-glow-of-a-great-reign-fo:
The After-Glow of a Great Reign collects four addresses given after the death of Queen Victoria. Speakers looked back on her long reign and what it had meant to Britain. The addresses mix praise, mourning, and moral teaching in the manner of sermons.

One speaker takes up a hard question from his text and answers it first. The answer, he says, comes from one who understood human nature, who had sinned and been forgiven. Such turns show how the addresses use scripture and the late queen's example together, to steady a nation in its grief.
20585-sartor-resartus-and-on-heroes-hero:
Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus and On Heroes appear together in this volume, his two most famous works. Sartor Resartus, or The Tailor Retailored, hides a philosophy of life inside a mad German professor's theory of clothes. On Heroes gathers Carlyle's lectures on hero worship through history.

Carlyle loves vast facts. Our theory of gravitation is as good as perfect, he writes. Lagrange has proved the planetary system will endure forever on this scheme, and Laplace guesses it could not have been made on any other. Such sweeps of science serve his real subject: the great souls who steer the world.
20643-the-character-and-influence-of-the:
The Character and Influence of the Indian Trade in Wisconsin is a scholarly study of the fur trade and its effects. It follows the trade from the French era into American hands. Trade goods, posts, and credit bound Native nations and European empires together across the Great Lakes.

The study opens with the broad forces at work. It considers what follows when a higher and a lower civilization meet in commerce, to use its period terms. The Phoenicians, it notes, built trade into a great historic agency, closely tied to piracy at first. Wisconsin's trade is then judged against that long history.
20713-a-campfire-girl-s-first-council-fi:
Jane L. Stewart's A Camp Fire Girl's First Council Fire opens her series about the Camp Fire Girls, the girls' organization founded alongside the Boy Scouts. Its heroine, Bessie, works as a hired girl before the Camp Fire changes her life. The first scenes show her home burden plainly.

There were tears in Bessie's eyes as she went at her dishes. Mrs. Hoover glared at her for a minute, then turned and left the kitchen, muttering about ingratitude. Against that drudgery, the council fire of the title offers friendship, ceremony, and the outdoors. The series sold the new movement to girl readers.
20833-exciting-adventures-of-mister-robe:
Sticks, grass, and mud build Mister Robert Robin's nest in a big basswood fork. Ben Field, in this 1928 tale, hides it so well that none below can spot it. From that safe perch, the robin family's adventures unfold for young readers.

Field wrote nature tales that teach while they charm small children. Robin parents feed, guard, and school their young through the season. Foes, storms, and first flights supply the small thrills. The plain, warm telling suits reading aloud, and its bird lore rests on close watching of real robin life in American yards and woods.
20868-cat-and-dog-or-memoirs-of-puss-and:
Puss the cat looks back on a life of more joy than grief in Cat and Dog. Constant kindness, the cat says, made that happy sum. Memoirs of Puss and the Captain lets two pets tell their own tales.

Mary Martha Sherwood wrote improving tales that mixed fun with moral care. Here, cat and dog recount masters, homes, and scrapes in turn. Animal voices let her teach kindness to beasts by stealth, in warm early children's writing. The tale is told for young readers. Both pets tell their tales in the first person.
20873-albert-gallatin:
No European-born citizen, says this 1883 life, rose higher in American service than Albert Gallatin. His gifts in lawmaking, finance, and diplomacy won praise on both Atlantic shores. Men of science, too, held his name in high regard worldwide.

Henry Adams wrote this compact life of the great Treasury chief. Gallatin funded a young nation, haggled peace at Ghent, and studied native tongues. Adams, himself a sharp historian, keeps the tale lean and keen. The book still serves as a crisp first path into the life of a founder too often left in Jefferson's shade.
21307-fire-island-being-the-adventures-o:
The Planet rides a tremendous sea in the eastern oceans as George Manville Fenn's tale opens. Her crew cling on while Mr Lane advises a life belt. A party of naturalists has shipped aboard her, bound for the island of the title. Their science offers no protection from what waits there.

Chapter after chapter drops the little group and their sailors into fresh danger, with the reader left guessing how each problem can be solved. Fenn was at his best in this mode. Uncertain naturalists face a remote island and perils from sea, weather, beasts, and men, right up to the closing chapters.
21348-benjamin-franklin:
John T. Morse Jr. wrote this life of Benjamin Franklin for the American Statesmen series, published in Boston in 1899. Fifteen chapters run from Franklin's early years through his life as a Philadelphia citizen. They continue through his two missions to England and his years as minister to France. The Hutchinson letters affair and the Privy Council scene get a chapter of their own.

Later chapters cover his financing work and his habits of life and business. The peace talks and his last years at home follow, ending with the Constitutional Convention and his death. Illustrations include Franklin's portrait and Independence Hall. Morse aimed at a compact political life for general readers, in the standard series of its day.
21463-voyages-and-travels-of-count-funni:
Count Funnibos and Baron Stilkin set out to see the world in W. H. G. Kingston's comic tale for the young. The two elderly nobles plan a grand voyage of discovery. In fact, their travels never take them beyond Holland, the land they start from.

Mishaps pile up, the pair part, and chance brings them back together. The Baron vows never to let a problem stop him, however daft his plan. One boot shared between two travellers is a fair sample of the logic. Kingston, rarely comic in his sea tales, here writes pure farce, with many pictures to match.
21654-in-and-around-berlin:
Minerva Brace Norton, an American living abroad, describes Berlin in In and Around Berlin, published in 1889. The approach to the city recalls the newer parts of New York, she writes. There the likeness ends, for Berlin is the heart of a very different nation.

Chapters treat family and social life, education, churches, and museums. The Reichstag and the Prussian Parliament get a chapter, as do famed personages. Norton dedicates the book to her countrymen who have visited Berlin, hope to go, or travel by armchair. Her Berlin is the stiff, bright capital of the young German Empire.
21821-the-mark-of-cain:
A duty dinner at the Olympic Club opens Andrew Lang's novel The Mark of Cain, published in 1886. Maitland of St. Gatien's watches his twenty guests linger over wine and olives, wishing they would go. Even at his own party he feels like an outsider. A strong hand on his shoulder wakes him from his reverie among the scattered fruit.

Lang, known for fairy tales and essays, here tries the modern novel of clubs and society. The title hints at a brand of guilt or fate that a man carries through polite life. Tobacco smoke, cold streets, and close talk fill the opening world. The tale that follows works in Lang's lighter register, curiosity and irony over melodrama.
21842-the-boy-scouts-of-lenox-or-the-hik:
A new scout patrol takes shape in Lenox in this 1915 boys' novel by Frank V. Webster. Tom Chesney, George Cooper, and Carl Oskamp count noses among themselves and find nearly a full patrol. George ought to make a fair scout, his friends allow, even if he is always finding fault. Their big test is the hike over Big Bear Mountain.

The frontispiece shows a rescue, with a boy hoisted to a limb while the next is hauled up. Webster wrote dozens of brisk books for boys, from farm lads to airship pilots. This one rides the first wave of the scouting craze. Woods craft, teamwork, and cheerful grit carry the troop over the mountain and back.
21968-the-finer-grain:
Late tales by Henry James fill The Finer Grain, published in 1910, five stories of success, visits, and quiet desolation. The Velvet Glove opens the book: novelist John Berridge, drunk on his prodigious hit, is sought out in Paris by a young lord. The lord begs the celebrity's judgment on a literary case. Berridge reads the whole scene as one more quaint act on the stage of European society.

A Round of Visits, Crapy Cornelia, and The Bench of Desolation follow in the contents. One tale, Mora Montravers, is missing pages in this text and was removed, as the note explains. James's late style is dense and circling, built for readers who savor motive over event. The finer grain of his title is the grain of feeling itself.
22041-mary-rose-of-mifflin:
Frances R. Sterrett published Mary Rose of Mifflin in 1910. Mary Rose is an orphan, the only child of her aunt's dead sister. When the girl needs a home, her aunt insists on taking her in. Her husband Larry Donovan grumbles at the plan, and the small town of Mifflin watches to see how it will end.

A child who has known little kindness changes the house she enters. Sterrett builds the tale from small scenes, neighbours, and slow softening of hearts. The fight is never about money or villains, only about whether a gruff man can learn to love a child. It is a gentle domestic novel of its period.
22230-hortus-inclusus-messages-from-the-:
John Ruskin wrote Hortus Inclusus as letters to the ladies of the Thwaite at Coniston. The Latin title means "a garden enclosed," and the subtitle calls the pieces messages from the wood to the garden. Ruskin sent them in happy days and dedicated the book to his dear friends in gratitude. They are among the gentlest things the great critic ever wrote.

The letters wander from flowers and woods to womanhood and the names of living creatures. Ruskin finds a small Paradise in a Lake District garden and in the friends who kept it. Late in life his prose here turns soft and grateful. The book is a quiet corner of his vast collected works.
22304-nicanor-teller-of-tales-a-story-of:
Nicanor, Teller of Tales is a story of Roman Britain by C. Bryson Taylor. Even its back matter shows the care behind the tale. A glossary pairs Roman place names with the British places they became.

Readers can match Abus with the Humber River and Tamesis with the Thames. Corinium becomes Cirencester, and Isca Silurum becomes Caerleon. Such a list tells you the fiction rests on a real Roman map. The story brings that occupied Britain to life through its teller, Nicanor. History readers get both a tale and a small gazetteer of Roman Britain in one volume.
22337-history-of-the-moors-of-spain:
History of the Moors of Spain tells how Muslim rulers shaped the Spanish peninsula. The French original had long enjoyed a high reputation. An American lady made the translation offered here.

Her taste and learning, the preface says, well fitted her for the task. Of all Muslim peoples, the Moors of Spain stood renowned in arts and arms. Their story fills the following pages in full. Readers meet a Spain of conquest, courts, and learning. The book also recalls the revival of learning in later medieval centuries. It remains a period account of a civilization that left deep marks on Spain.
22345-memoirs-of-the-private-life-return:
Memoirs of the Private Life, Return, and Reign of Napoleon concerns the emperor in 1815. That was the year of his return from exile and final reign. The writer promises facts that merit close attention from readers.

Study shows a character full of contrasts, the memoir argues. Napoleon appears by turns mistrustful and open, ardent and reserved. He is enterprising yet irresolute, vindictive yet generous. He favors liberty and yet acts the despot. Such a portrait refuses simple praise or blame. Readers get an insider's view of the Hundred Days. It remains useful for anyone tracing how contemporaries judged Napoleon's baffling mix of gifts.
22550-old-mackinaw-or-the-fortress-of-th:
Old Mackinaw, or the Fortress of the Lakes, recounts Michigan's straits country. Mackinac stood guard where Lakes Huron and Michigan meet. Its bibliography alone shows the depth of sources behind the history.

Schoolcraft's works, in three volumes, stand among the chief sources. Shea's Catholic Missions and Discovery of the Mississippi also appear. Lanman's History of Michigan and Parkman's Siege of Pontiac are listed. Foster and Whitney's Geological Report covers the land itself in science. Ferris's Great West and Disturnell's Trip to the Lakes add travel accounts. Readers get a fortress town's story built from many witnesses. French missions, British guns, and American trade all passed that island.
22737-john-gayther-s-garden-and-the-stor:
John Gayther's Garden and the Stories Told Therein is a story collection built around an old gardener and the tales his garden draws out of him; it appeared in 1902. The catalog record names no author. The frame is simple and warm: a garden, its keeper, and the people who pass through it.

John Gayther did not own the garden; he only had charge of it. At busy seasons he had men to help him. For most of the year, though, he preferred to do everything himself. That modest opening sets the book's pace: work, weather, and talk among the beds. Stories told therein grow naturally from the place. Readers who enjoy frame tales and quiet village worlds will find a gentle specimen here.
22874-frank-merriwell-s-pursuit-or-how-t:
Burt L. Standish sends Frank Merriwell into danger in Frank Merriwell's Pursuit, published in 1904. The talk in the excerpt runs hot. Lives hang on the outcome, one man insists. He offers money for aid and asks, practically, whether the house holds any whisky. Merriwell tales rarely pause for breath.

Frank was the clean-living Yale hero of a hugely popular dime-novel series. Each adventure tested his nerve, honesty, and athletic skill against plotters who played dirty. How to Win, the subtitle, states the formula plainly. Modern readers meet here a piece of the reading that shaped American boys a century ago. The values are dated, the pace is not, and the period flavor is the real attraction.
22912-phyllis-a-twin:
Dorothy Whitehill's Phyllis, a Twin, published in 1920, opens in sunshine off Fifth Avenue. In a house a short distance from Central Park, every window stands open. Soft white curtains flutter in a crisp breeze, and cool yellow light floods the rooms. A girls' story could hardly ask for a brighter start.

Phyllis shares her life with a twin, and twinship drives the fun and the mix-ups of this series for young readers. School, friends, and small adventures fill the chapters in the manner of the period's girls' books. Whitehill keeps the tone bright and the stakes friendly. The volume preserves a whole style of wholesome series fiction, written to be passed hand to hand among sisters and friends.
22921-the-death-and-burial-of-cock-robin:
Who'll carry him to his grave, asks The Death and Burial of Cock Robin. The Kite volunteers to bear the body to burial, so long as daylight lasts. The Linnet offers to fetch a torch and carry the light for the procession. So the old rhyme calls its mourners one by one.

Bird after bird takes a part in the burial, the Lark serving as clerk and saying Amen. The verses have taught children rhyme and rhythm for centuries, and picture editions made the procession famous. This printing pairs the familiar questions and answers with illustrations. It is a nursery classic in its simplest form, solemn and playful at once, and built to be read aloud.
23012-elder-conklin:
A girl refuses plainly in Elder Conklin, Frank Harris's story of frontier courtship. Why, just the plainest kind of refusal, I guess, she says. She told the other man only that she felt bound to go with a stranger instead. The refusal, she insists, could not have been plainer. Afraid, she repeats, as if the word stung her. But he'll lose nothing by waiting, nothing. You hear me talk. And her eyes flashed.

The flash promises the story's real subject, a young woman managing rival claims in a raw settlement. Elder Conklin's name carries the respectability she is weighing against a stranger's pull. Harris builds the scene almost wholly from talk, and the talk crackles. His western women rarely wait quietly to be chosen, and this one states her terms herself.
23023-notes-and-queries-number-201-septe:
Notes and Queries, number 201, dated September 3, 1853, trades in literary suspicion. One note quotes a warning about Swinney, a wretched but dangerous fool. He had the impudence, the writer says, to go to Lord G. Sackville, a stranger to him, and ask outright whether he was the author of Junius, the famous anonymous letters. Take care of him, the note ends.

That appetite for attribution fills the whole weekly number. Readers sent questions on books, proverbs, families, and forgotten facts, and other readers answered them. The journal called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men and artists. Bound runs became a Victorian reference web in print. This single number preserves the correspondence mid-flow, quarrels and all.
a-brief-history-of-panics-and-their-peri: Clément Juglar's brief history of panics traces America's financial crashes and their rhythm. His pioneering work founded the study of business cycles. Economics history of lasting value. His Juglar cycles still figure in every economics textbook. Boom and bust march through his pages in fateful rhythm.
a-heap-o-livin: Guest's Heap o' Livin' (1916) celebrates everyday joys in homely verse. Optimism reigns. The Tower library holds the full text. It heaped living. Days glowed. Smiles spread. Hearts warmed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
agobard-de-grandine-et-tonitruis-latin:
Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, wrote his book on hail and thunder around 815, in the age of Charlemagne's heirs. The Latin treatise attacks a belief common among his flock. Farmers held that weather magicians, called tempestarii, raised storms and sold the stolen crops to sky sailors.

Agobard calls the belief folly and proves it from Scripture and reason. He tells of a crowd ready to stone supposed sky travelers, whom he talked down himself. His work is the earliest systematic church attack on folk magic. Theologians quoted him for a thousand years. The Latin text preserves a bishop thinking clearly against the panic of his own parish.
agrippa-de-occulta-philosophia-1533-lati:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa published his Three Books of Occult Philosophy in Latin at Cologne in 1533, the first full edition. The work is the foundational synthesis of Renaissance magic. Astrology, Kabbalah, number lore, and natural magic all find their ordered place in Agrippa's vast system.

Book by book, he rises from the elemental world through the celestial to the divine. Every later magus drank from this spring, and most admitted the debt. The Latin text of 1533 is the form in which Europe first read him. Agrippa aimed to restore magic as a learned, pious discipline. His bible of Renaissance magic still anchors any serious study of the occult tradition.
agrippa-de-vanitate-1564-latin:
Agrippa published On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences in 1530, and this Latin edition of 1564 kept his great skeptical performance in print. The book demolishes the arts and sciences one by one. Grammar, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself all stand accused of vanity and error.

The joke cuts deep, since Agrippa's own Occult Philosophy had taught several of these arts. Readers have debated for centuries how much of the attack he meant. As rhetoric, the De vanitate is a masterpiece of learned doubt. As a companion to the Occult Philosophy, it is unmatched: learn magic first, Agrippa seems to say, then learn to doubt everything, including the lesson.
albumasar-introductorium-1489-latin:
Abu Ma'shar of Baghdad, called Albumasar in Latin, wrote the Great Introduction to astrology in the ninth century. It became the book that taught the Latin West the Arabic system of the art. Hermann of Dalmatia turned it into Latin, and the version here was printed in 1489. No English version in the public domain exists.

Albumasar grounds the power of the stars in physics, sorting signs, planets, houses, and aspects into one great scheme. Kings and scholars across Europe used his book to read the heavens for three centuries. The printed Latin of 1489 shows the work at the height of its fame. It stands as the record of how Arabic astrology remade a science in the West.
alcabitius-isagoge-1521-latin:
Al-Qabisi, a scholar of Aleppo in the tenth century, wrote the Isagoge as a short first book for students of astrology. For the rest of the Middle Ages it served as the standard beginner's text in the Latin West. The edition here is the Latin printing from Venice in 1521, with the commentary of John of Saxony.

Five chapters lay out the signs, the planets, the houses, and the terms a judge of the stars must know. John of Saxony, a Paris master of the 1300s, explains each point for the classroom. No English version in the public domain exists. The little book shows how a whole science was taught, one clear rule at a time.
allan-quatermain:
H. Rider Haggard sent his hunter hero Allan Quatermain on his last trek in this book of 1887. It is the mate to King Solomon's Mines, the hit of two years past. Haggard wrote it while the fame of the first book was still fresh and high.

Quatermain, now old, joins a last hunt for a lost white race in the heart of Africa. Strange priests, a vast cave world, and a doom that hangs on the band fill the tale. The book turns the brisk hunter of the first tale into a figure of myth.
annals-and-reminiscences-of-jamaica-plai: Harriet Manning Whitcomb gathers the annals of Jamaica Plain — the Boston suburb's old houses, families, and changing ways. Local history lovingly told. A treasure for all who love New England's past. Old families, vanished customs, and the growth of a Boston suburb live again in her affectionate pages.
augustine-de-divinatione-daemonum-latin:
Augustine of Hippo wrote De divinatione daemonum, on the divination of demons, around 413. The short Latin treatise asks a sharp question. If demons foretell the future truly, as pagans claimed, why must Christians refuse their oracles?

Augustine answers that demons guess shrewdly rather than know. Keen senses, long memory, and swift travel let them predict much, he argues. Their hits prove no divine gift, and their aim is to trap human souls. The treatise became foundational for all medieval demonology. Later writers on witchcraft built on Augustine's frame. Here it stands in its original Latin, brief and decisive.
bacon-epistola-secretis-1618-latin:
Roger Bacon, the thirteenth-century Franciscan, addressed his Letter on the Secret Works of Art and Nature to a learned reader of his day. John Dee edited this Latin printing of 1618, a fitting match of editor and author. The epistle ranges over marvels, magic, and natural philosophy in Bacon's bold voice.

Bacon describes wonders that art and nature can work without demons. Flying machines, great ships, and burning mirrors pass in review as things knowledge might achieve. He writes like a prophet of experimental science. Dee, who owned more Bacon manuscripts than anyone, gave the letter to the press. Readers meet the medieval friar whom later ages turned into a magician, arguing here for nature's hidden powers.
brentano-das-marchen-von-dem-myrtenfraul:
Clemens Brentano wove Italian folk material into his fairy tale of the myrtle maiden, Das Maerchen von dem Myrtenfraeulein, given here in German. A plant, a maiden, and a secret life hidden inside green leaves carry the story. Brentano was the most musical of the German Romantics, and his tales sing on the page.

Love and transformation govern the plot, as folk wonders receive a poet's lush retelling. The marvelous feels natural in Brentano's hands, which is the fairy tale's oldest trick done perfectly. Readers of German will hear his verbal music at full strength. The tale shows why his name anchors the Romantic fairy tale. Small in size, the piece holds a whole enchanted garden inside it.
bruno-de-magia-latin:
Giordano Bruno wrote De Magia, on magic, in Latin near the end of his wandering life, around 1590. Bruno treats magic as the art of bonds. All things, he argues, are linked by attractions and sympathies, and the magus works by knowing and pulling those links.

 His system sorts magic into kinds and traces how images, words, and desires bind souls. The treatise is the philosophical peak of Renaissance magic theory. Bruno the thinker of infinite worlds stands behind every page. Burned at Rome in 1600, he left this calm, daring account of his art. Readers meet the mind for which the cosmos itself was the great web of bonds.
c-f-meyer-die-richterin:
A woman holds the power of justice in Charlemagne's age and must judge her own family's crimes. C. F. Meyer's Die Richterin, given here in German, builds its tragedy around Stemma, the judge of its title. Few heroines in German fiction carry her sternness and sorrow in equal measure.

Guilt and atonement govern the plot, as hidden sins surface under her own tribunal. Meyer writes the early medieval world with his usual lapidary force, every scene cut clean. Stemma's strength is real, and so is the price it exacts from her heart. Critics call the novella the master's late masterpiece. Magnificently written, it closes his career on a note of stern, tragic grandeur.
canon-episcopi-latin:
The Canon Episcopi is a church law text from around 900, passed down through Regino of Prüm's collection. It treats the belief that certain women ride at night with Diana or Herodias. The canon declares the night flight an illusion worked by demons, not a bodily fact.

That ruling mattered for centuries. Canon lawyers quoted the text for six hundred years, and it long held back full-blown witch persecution. Later demonologists had to argue around its plain denial. The canon shows the early medieval church as the skeptic in the room. Its Latin lines are brief, but few texts on witchcraft have been cited more often or fought over harder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-lehn: The Encyclopedia's Lehnin entry: the Cistercian house of Brandenburg's sands. Grey monks tamed the wilderness. Richard Urban Butler writes its story. Prayer in the pine woods. The prophecy of Lehnin made its name famous in legend. Its brick church stands among the pines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abthain: This 1913 reference piece on the abthain — the old Scottish church office, half abbot, half steward. Thomas Walsh explains its Celtic roots. Land and prayer met in the title. A relic of the early Scottish Church. Its lands passed to lay lords at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adele-amalie-: This 1913 reference piece on Princess Gallitzin — Adele Amalie, the German convert of Münster. Patricius Schlager tells her story. Her salon became a Catholic circle. Goethe mourned her going to Rome. A soul that found its home. Her son became a missionary in America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-akhmin: This 1913 reference piece on Akhmin — the old Egyptian city of the Copts. Henri Leclercq notes its Christian past. Martyrs bled in its pagan temples. The Nile guards its ancient stones. A Pharaonic town turned Christian. Its papyri enrich the world's museums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-jean-b: This 1913 reference article on Albert Belin — a French churchman of letters. Alexius Hoffmann notes his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. A writer in the Church's service. His books served the faithful. His sermons edified the faithful. His diocese mourned a devoted shepherd.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albrecht-von-: A 1913 entry on Wallenstein — the imperial general of the Thirty Years' War. Martin Spahn tells his meteoric tale. His armies were states on the march. Eger's assassins ended his dreams. The warlord of the German tragedy. His palace in Prague keeps his memory.

Thomas Erastus, the Swiss Reformed doctor and theologian, wrote this Repetition of the Disputation on Witches at Basel in 1578. The Latin text answers Johann Weyer, the great skeptic who held that accused witches were melancholy women fooled by the devil, not partners with him. Their clash is the great sixteenth-century debate on the reality of witchcraft.

Erastus grants the devil real power and urges the death penalty for true witches, yet even he trims the wildest charges of the witch hunters. He writes as both physician and churchman, and the two callings pull against each other on the page. The book marks the limit of skepticism in its age. Weyer lost the round, and the burnings went on.

errores-gazariorum-latin:
The Errores Gazariorum is an anonymous Latin treatise from Savoy, written around 1430. Its title means the errors of the Cathars, a name now pinned on supposed witches. Scholars prize it as the founding document of the witches' sabbath, the first full description of that fateful idea.

The text describes secret night assemblies where heretics renounce Christ and feast with demons. Before this treatise, such elements lay scattered in separate charges. Here they fuse into the sabbath stereotype whole. That stereotype would condemn thousands across the next two centuries. Cold, brief, and fateful, the Savoyard text marks the moment the witch of legend took her lasting shape.
eymerich-directorium-inquisitorum-1578-l:
Nicholas Eymerich, inquisitor of Aragon, wrote the Directorium Inquisitorum in 1376, the manual that taught inquisitors their trade for two hundred years. The text here is the Rome edition of 1578, with the commentaries of Francisco Peña. Eymerich wrote from a hard life of hunting heresy in Catalonia and at the papal court.

The manual covers the whole craft: how heresy is found, how witnesses are heard, how torture is ruled, and how sentences are framed. Its sections on witchcraft and sorcery later fed the Malleus tradition of the witch trials. Peña's notes bring the old text up to the age of the Spanish Inquisition. It is the procedural root of the early modern persecution.
facts-and-arguments-for-darwin: German naturalist Fritz Müller, working in Brazil, wrote this early and powerful defense of Darwin's theory of evolution. A key document from the years when evolution was still fighting for acceptance.
ficino-de-vita-1529-latin:
Marsilio Ficino, the Florentine priest-philosopher, wrote his Three Books on Life in the fifteenth century. This Latin edition of 1529 spread his manual of astrological medicine and natural magic. Ficino taught how the planets shape the body, and how a scholar might live long under their influence.

Diet, music, scents, and stones all enter his regimen for the learned life. He writes for melancholy scholars like himself, in danger from their own desks. The book is the philosophical root of learned Renaissance magic. Physicians and magi read it side by side for generations. Ficino's Florence speaks here: Platonism turned into a daily art of health.
ficino-de-vita-libri-tres-1498-latin:
Marsilio Ficino, the leading thinker of Florence's Platonic Academy, wrote Three Books on Life in 1489. The Latin text here comes from the Venice edition of 1498. The work is a guide to health for scholars, built on astrology, medicine, and natural magic.

Ficino teaches readers how to guard their health, live long, and draw strength from the planets and stars. He covers diet, sleep, herbs, music, and talismans, the images meant to catch heavenly power. The book, with its added defense of his magic, became the base work of Renaissance medical astrology.
ficino-pimander-1481-latin:
In 1463 Marsilio Ficino set aside his Plato to translate a Greek manuscript that had just reached Florence: the discourses of Hermes Trismegistus. His Latin version, the Pimander, was printed in 1481. It lit the Hermetic fever of the Renaissance. No English version of Ficino's own text exists in the public domain.

The discourses tell of God as light and life, the making of the world, and the fall and return of man. Ficino and his readers took Hermes for a sage older than Moses, a gentile prophet of Christian truth. The book reshaped Renaissance thought on magic, the soul, and the stars. This early printing is the form in which Europe first read it.
gerson-de-erroribus-artem-magicam-1402-l:
Jean Gerson, chancellor of the University of Paris, wrote De Erroribus circa Artem Magicam in 1402. The Latin title means, in plain words, on the errors that gather around the magic art. The text here comes from the 1706 collected works issued under Dupin.

Gerson lists the mistakes he saw in charms, spells, and claims of hidden power, and judges them by church teaching. He wrote early, before the great witch trials of later years had taken shape. His short treatise shows a leading church scholar drawing a firm line around magic. It marks an opening move in a long debate.

Groups asked the International Criminal Court to investigate company executives for facilitating crimes against humanity. That makes the papers more than corporate history. They became evidence in a filing that tests whether business leaders can be held criminally responsible for paying armed groups in a war zone.

Payments by Chiquita Brands in Colombia are the subject of this National Security Archive page, built on the company's own papers. The documents total more than 800,000 dollars paid to Colombian guerrillas. That figure comes from the records themselves, not from outside estimates.

Company payments to armed groups in Colombia later drew criminal cases and fines in the United States. A paper trail this detailed lets readers follow amounts and recipients directly. It is primary evidence for how a major fruit company financed fighters during Colombia's long internal conflict. The amount gave investigators a fixed starting point for wider inquiries.

The page documents a transparency win whose contents researchers can now request and read.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_New:
A recently declassified document on the 1953 Iran coup makes a charged claim about the coup's Iranian helpers. Malcolm Byrne and Mark Gasiorowski edited this briefing book, posted in March 2018. The passage alleges that senior Iranian clerics received large sums of money from the United States.

Clerical involvement has long been debated by historians of the coup against Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Money flowing to religious leaders would help explain street mobilization against him. A single declassified passage does not settle the debate, but it adds a concrete document where mostly inference existed before, and scholars of 1953 will have to weigh it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_The:
Thirty years after the Iran-Contra affair broke, Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, number 567, published in November 2016. Declassified records recall official deception carried out in the name of protecting a presidency. The affair joined secret arms sales to Iran with illegal support for Nicaraguan rebels.

The posting calls Iran-Contra a milestone in post-truth politics. That framing argues the scandal taught later officials that surviving a story could matter more than telling the truth. The documents let readers test that claim against memos and testimony from the cover-up itself, rather than taking the anniversary judgment on faith.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In the autumn of 1991, President George H.W. Bush announced unilateral withdrawals of American nuclear weapons. This briefing book, posted in September 2016, covers that pullback and the answer it drew from Moscow. The Soviet Union matched the move with rapid cuts of its own.

Unilateral means Washington did not wait for a treaty or a negotiation. It simply withdrew whole classes of weapons and invited a response. That gamble produced one of the fastest nuclear reductions of the Cold War, weeks before the Soviet Union itself dissolved. The documents show disarmament by announcement, a method arms control rarely attempts.

In 1957 the CIA debriefed a witness who had seen a Soviet hydrogen bomb test up close. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 623, published in April 2018. It presents newly declassified intelligence reports from 1957 on Soviet atomic development.

The witness described air crackling with pressure, as if the air was tearing up. CIA analysis also credited German scientists with greatly accelerating Soviet nuclear research. Eyewitness color of that kind is rare in intelligence files, which usually trade in estimates and photographs. The reports show analysts piecing together a rival's bomb program from human fragments in the years before satellites.

Greenland's size and position made it vital to American defense in the early Cold War, and nuclear plans followed. This briefing book is the first part of a series on episodes in that nuclear history, from 1947 to 1968. Its named landmark is Thule Air Base, the early-warning site in the far north.

Evidence gives the span and the Thule focus, and the description stays within them. Radar at Thule watched for Soviet bombers and missiles over the pole, which put a Danish territory inside America's nuclear warning system. The episodes collected here show how a quiet Arctic island became a working part of the superpower standoff.

In September 1979 a flash over the South Atlantic raised the question of a secret nuclear test, and the event became known as the Vela Incident. This briefing-book page presents the Archive's record under that name. A fuller companion volume, The Vela Flash, prints a CIA judgment putting the chance of a test at ninety percent or more. The evidence here is the title alone. This page is the shorter entry point to a mystery that governments have never officially solved.

Iceland sat astride the North Atlantic sea lanes, yet no American nuclear weapons were ever deployed there during the Cold War. This briefing book, posted in August 2016, shows how close the question came to a different answer. A recently declassified State Department record documents the internal debate.

Officials debated whether to deploy the weapons in Iceland, including through secret deployments hidden from the Icelanders. A secret deployment in a democratic ally that opposed such weapons would have carried real political danger. The record matters because the debate happened at all: geography kept pulling planners toward a country whose consent was doubtful, and restraint, in the end, won.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
What Boris Yeltsin heard from Western leaders about NATO expansion became a lasting Russian grievance. This briefing book, posted in March 2018, publishes declassified documents from the American side and others on those conversations. Its companion volume covers what Gorbachev heard a few years earlier.

Evidence here is a truncated dateline, so the description must stay general. The subject itself is precise: exact words spoken to a Russian president about whether NATO would move east. Transcripts and memos let readers compare those assurances with later claims from both sides. In a dispute where memory is the battlefield, paper is the only referee.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_vietnam_:
South Vietnamese president Ngo Dinh Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963, with American knowledge. Briefing Book number 730, edited by John Prados and Luke Nichter and published in November 2020, brings new evidence to that old event, including material from President John Kennedy's own files.

A newly released Kennedy tape and the president's intelligence checklists fill gaps in the known record. They suggest Kennedy leaned toward regime change more strongly than earlier accounts believed. Most striking are notes by Diem himself, published for the first time, written hours before his assassination. For readers, the release sharpens the hardest question of the Vietnam story's first act: how far did Washington go in toppling its own ally?
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Explo: Russian social media operations around the 2017 violence in Charlottesville, Virginia became a case study in how foreign influence campaigns exploit American divisions. A National Security Archive briefing book page gathers its material under the heading of exploring that campaign. It covers the posts, pages, and provocations attributed to Russian operators. They appeared as a white supremacist rally turned deadly. Only the page capture survives here. Its subject remains significant, because Charlottesville showed influence work aimed not at an election directly but at a wound in American public life.
greifenstein: F. Marion Crawford sets this dramatic novel among the German aristocracy, in the shadow of the ancient castle of Greifenstein. Pride, family honor, and a tragic secret drive the von Greifenstein family toward a shattering reckoning. Crawford's cosmopolitan storytelling — he wrote of half the countries of Europe — gives the tale both grandeur and intimate feeling.
harvey-de-motu-cordis-latin:
William Harvey proves the blood's circuit in his Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis, in Latin from 1628. The heart works as a pump, driving blood in an endless round. Valves, ligatures, and vivisection build his case step by careful step in the most important medical book ever written by an Englishman.

Harvey counts the blood's volume and shows no other path is possible. Galen's old system, master for fourteen centuries, falls before his trials. The slim Latin volume remade physiology from the ground up at once. Readers meet modern medicine at its birth, in the author's own words, argued with a clarity that still instructs.
isidore-etymologiae-latin:
Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled the Etymologiae in the seventh century to save the learning of the ancient world. This text is the full Latin work in W. M. Lindsay's Oxford edition of 1911. Twenty books hold nearly all the knowledge a medieval reader could reach.

Isidore explains words and things together, from grammar and law to stones, ships, and food. Book Eleven treats man and the monster races of the far East. Book Twelve covers beasts, the seed of every later bestiary. Monasteries copied the work for centuries. It is the Middle Ages' own encyclopedia, and its wonders fed a thousand years of marvels.
judgments-of-the-court-of-appeal-of-new-:
Judgments of the Court of Appeal of New Zealand records the court's ruling on the Mount Erebus aircraft disaster inquiry. The case number is C.A. 95/81. Air New Zealand and two officials applied to review parts of the Royal Commission's report. Justice Peter Mahon, who ran the inquiry, was first respondent.

The full bench sat: Woodhouse, Cooke, Richardson, McMullin, and Somers. Hearings ran on October 5 through 9 and 12, 1981. Counsel appeared for the airline, the pilots' association, the Attorney-General, and the Civil Aviation Division. The document gives the court's judgments on how far a royal commission's findings could stand. It is a legal record of one of New Zealand's gravest public disputes.
keziah-coffin:
Keziah Coffin is a novel by Joseph C. Lincoln, set in the Cape Cod village of Trumet. Every chapter title begins the same way: 'In which Keziah...' She talks with the parson, argues with Captain Nat, and opposes Captain Eben. The brig Sea Mist sails in chapter five, and Trumet talks in chapter six.

Keziah receives unexpected callers, visits Kyan Pepper's shop, and dresses a doll. Her next-door neighbor makes a call, and discord sounds in the parish. Captain Eben tells a story, and Keziah falls from grace in her neighbors' eyes. A last chapter tells who Keziah sees and what she does. Lincoln builds a whole village comedy around one sharp-tongued, warm-hearted Cape Cod woman.
king-olaf-s-kinsman-a-story-of-the-last-:
King Olaf's Kinsman is Charles W. Whistler's story of the last Saxon struggle against the Danes. His preface notes that no English chronicler mentions King Olaf coming to England. Yet two churches, one at each end of London Bridge, testify to his presence. Whistler fits Olaf's deeds from the Saga of King Olaf the Holy into the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's order.

That order runs from Swein's death to the accession of Cnut. A hard fight at Ringmereheath gets a Suffolk home in his retelling. Whistler imagines an English kinsman of Olaf telling the tale from inside the saga world. His novels of Saxon England always rested on this kind of chronicle checking. This one braids Norse saga and English record into a single adventure.
lectures-on-art-delivered-before-the-uni:
John Ruskin delivered these Lectures on Art at Oxford in Hilary term, 1870. The contents list an inaugural lecture first. Then come art's relation to religion, and art's relation to morals.

Ruskin had just become Oxford's first Slade Professor of Fine Art. He used the chair to preach art as a moral force. Students heard that drawing trains both eye and character. Later lectures treat landscape and Greek art in the full series. These talks helped shape British art education for a generation. Dana, his editor, was a noted author himself. Their friendship helped preserve Allston's thought for American art.
letters-and-journals-of-james-eighth-ear:
The letters and journals of James Bruce, eighth Earl of Elgin, appeared after his death. Dean Stanley of Westminster supplied a preface. Elgin's family and friends consulted Stanley about publishing a record.

Stanley says Elgin's career touched many critical points of empire. Elgin governed in Canada and served in China and India. His letters mix public duty with private reflection. The journals show a Victorian statesman at close range. Readers of imperial history will find a candid, careful self-portrait here. Elgin's role in Canada fills much of the early record. His later China mission brought fame and controversy alike.
life-of-chopin:
Franz Liszt wrote this life of his fellow composer Chopin. Martha Walker Cook translated it from the French. The original edition appeared in 1863, the notes to this text explain. A fourth, revised edition of 1880 underlies this electronic version.

Cook dedicates her translation to Jan Pychowski, a Polish pianist. She praises his earnest patriotism, like Chopin's own. Liszt knew Chopin personally, which gives the memoir special weight. Seven chapters carry the pianist-composer's story in Liszt's romantic voice. Cookery of the text cut pages apart for scanning, its notes confess. She dedicated the work without Pychowski's consent or knowledge beforehand.
little-britain:
Washington Irving sketches a small London neighborhood in this piece. Little Britain hides among narrow streets and venerable houses. Christ Church School and St. Bartholomew's Hospital bound it westward. Smithfield, Long Lane, and Aldersgate Street frame its other sides.

St. Paul's dome looks down with motherly protection over it. The quarter once housed the Dukes of Brittany, Irving says. Fashion later rolled west, and trade took the deserted homes. For a time the district became a great mart of learning. Bull-and-Mouth Street's gulf separates it from Butcher Lane. Dukes of Brittany once resided in the ancient quarter.
looking-seaward-again:
Sir Walter Runciman published these sea tales in 1907. The Walter Scott Publishing Company issued them in London. He inscribes the fragments affectionately to his wife. His preface says the tales were told by firesides first.

Runciman claims only unvarnished matters of fact for them. Early desertion of home for sailing vessels limited his schooling. Steam was already taking the wind from sailing ships then. Contents promise torpedoes, ice, smugglers, and a Russian port. A pasha before Plevna and Dutchy and his chief appear. Fair trade and foul play open the contents' sea stories.
lord-dolphin:
Harriet A. Cheever published this children's sea story in 1903. Diantha W. Horne illustrated the volume. Lord Dolphin introduces himself in the first chapter. Under the waves and a coral grove follow quickly.

A mermaid's cave, gardens, and treasure grounds await young readers. The dolphin narrator reports what he saw one strange day. A great vessel strains and tugs in the frontispiece. His adventures end with a surprising visit onto land. Madame Angora and Mother Bunny preceded Cheever's dolphin tale. Billy Trill's strange adventures headline her earlier children's books. Cheever had written Madame Angora and Mother Bunny for children before.
lord-elgin:
Sir John George Bourinot wrote this life of Lord Elgin. The Makers of Canada series issued it at Toronto in 1903. Duncan Campbell Scott and Pelham Edgar edited the series. Bourinot finished and revised the pages shortly before his death.

Editors praise his breadth of political vision and factual mastery. Elgin's Canadian career required unusual insight into constitutional law. Contents cover the Indemnification Act and two ministries' ends. Clergy reserves, seigniorial tenure, and American relations close it. Farewell to Canada closes the ten-chapter contents list. Canada and the United States receive the ninth chapter's attention.
lord-kilgobbin:
Charles Lever sets this tale of Ireland at Kilgobbin Castle. It first ran as a serial in the Cornhill Magazine. Luke Fildes illustrated that run from October 1870 onward. Smith, Elder published the three-volume book form in 1872.

Lever dedicates it in breaking health and broken spirits. The task once his joy became linked with sorrow, he writes. Prince Kostalergi and the chums enter the castle's home life. A drive through a bog shows how friends may differ. The blue coat and the cousins follow the Trinity chapters. Kilgobbin Castle's home life anchors Lever's final novel.
marie-an-episode-in-the-life-of-the-late:
Marie is an episode in the life of Allan Quatermain by H. Rider Haggard. His dedication, dated at Ditchingham in 1912, recalls southern Africa. He lists the annexation of the Transvaal and the Zulu and Boer wars. Against that history he sets young Allan's first love.

Allan learns French, then rides to the rescue at Maraisfontein. Marie Marais is the girl whose farm is attacked. A shooting match, a parting, and a camp of death follow. Dingaan's bet and Retief's treaty bring the Great Trek into the tale. Haggard mourns the innocent blood of those years. The novel is a moving prequel for Quatermain's many readers.
mark-twain:
Mark Twain, by Archibald Henderson, is an early life of the humorist. Photographs by Alvin Langdon Coburn illustrate the volume. A poem by Bliss Carman pictures Twain jesting among the great dead. Henderson's preface speaks of a world in debt to Twain's humor.

His own feeling, he says, began in childhood with warm affection. It grew from the works first, then from knowing the man. Henderson traces the Hannibal boy who became a river pilot and miner. Newspaper work in the West sharpened the young humorist. World fame, the white suit, and the sage's drawl complete the portrait. The book glows with personal gratitude and knowledge.
martin-arles-tractatus-superstitionibus-:
Martin of Arles was a canon from Navarre who wrote a Latin treatise on superstition in 1517. The work was printed at Rome in 1559 under the title Tractatus de Superstitionibus. Its full title adds that it argues against harmful magic and sorcery, the twin fears named in Latin as maleficia and sortilegia.

Martin sorts the false beliefs and secret rites of his day and argues that clergy should correct them. He writes as a churchman close to daily parish life, not as a distant judge. The treatise stands between older pastoral teaching and the sharper demon manuals of the next century. Readers can see early modern fears of magic taking fixed, written form.
memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the Memoir of Fleeming Jenkin for Scribner's in 1901. Jenkin's kin meant to print his papers, with this life at their head. In America the life came out alone, without those papers.

Stevenson warns that Jenkin was more than his work shows. His force lay in friendship, in brave views of life, and in hard thought. Chapter one traces the Jenkins of Stowting and Fleeming's father at sea. Stevenson wrote the preface at Saranac in October 1887. St. Helena and King Tom stand in his father's sea tale. A life of cables and college work grows from those roots.
morgagni-sedibus-1761-latin:
Latin was still the tongue of learned medicine when Morgagni issued De sedibus in 1761. The full title promises five books on the seats and causes of diseases, studied by anatomy. This Latin first edition holds the complete original text. Its final line, Finis Tomi Secundi, closes the second Latin tome.

Morgagni spent decades gathering cases from Padua's hospitals and his own practice. He set each patient's story beside the autopsy that followed death. From that pairing grew modern pathology. An English translation by Alexander, in three volumes, is also held. Scholars use the Latin to check every term. The original carries an authority copies cannot match.
moths-of-the-limberlost-a-book-about-lim:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this nature book about the moths around her Limberlost Cabin in Indiana. She dedicates it to Neltje Degraff Doubleday. The first chapters cover moths generally: their eggs, caterpillars, and winter quarters. Then the book takes up species one by one, under the folk names she loved.

The Robin Moth, the Yellow Emperor, and the Lady Bird get chapters. So do the Moths of the Moon, the King of the Hollyhocks, and Hera of the Corn. Bloody-Nose of Sunshine Hill and the Modest Moth close the list. Stratton-Porter reared moths at home and photographed them, mixing science with storytelling.
muslin:
George Moore first published this Irish novel in 1886 as A Drama in Muslin. A new edition came out in September 1915. The tale opens at the Convent of the Holy Child. White-dressed schoolgirls flutter in the green garden like doves.

It is prize day, and a bishop's visit stirs the school. Plain Alice Barton has written the day's musical sketch. Moore watches the girls with a cool, close eye. Their dresses, hopes, and ranks all matter here. The novel follows convent girls into Dublin's marriage market. Moore's plain style was bold for its day, and the book made his name.
my-first-picture-book-with-thirty-six-pa:
Joseph Martin Kronheim printed this first picture book in rich colors. Routledge issued it in London and New York. It holds thirty-six pages of pictures for small children. A first alphabet leads the contents.

Old tales follow: the Old Woman in a Shoe, and Babes in the Wood. Little Bo-Peep and Five Little Pigs come next. Mother Goose and her son Jack close the set. Each letter pairs a word with a bright picture. Kronheim was a pioneer of color printing for children. The book shows Victorian picture books at their gayest, made to teach letters through charm.
my-robin:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells the true tale behind her famed robin. A reader of The Secret Garden wrote to ask one question. Had she owned the real robin from that book? Burnett says the letter thrilled her to the center of her being.

She answers that she did not own him at all. He owned her, or perhaps they owned each other. Her robin is the small English kind, not the American bird. He wears a red satin waistcoat on a plump breast. Each tilt of his head seems full of drama. Burnett's sketch is a love letter to one bold garden friend.
mysterious-mr-sabin:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this spy novel, copyrighted in 1905 by Little, Brown. Its first chapter is a supper party at the Milan. A drama of the pavement follows at once. Felix gives a warning in chapter three.

Chapter four moves to the Russian ambassador's rooms. A frontispiece shows a girl's face lit like fine statuary. The old text opens with a toast among men at supper. Densham lifts his glass under rose-shaded lights. Sabin, the mysterious man of the title, drives the intrigue. Oppenheim builds an early spy tale of plots, warnings, and high society masks.
nasa-tm-19630013134-stress-corrosion-of-:
T. S. Humphries of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on June 24, 1963. It studies stress corrosion in strong aluminum alloys. Stress corrosion cracks metal held under load in a harsh setting. The alloys named are 2014, 2024, 2219, 7075, 7178, and 7079.

Tests dipped samples in salt water, then exposed them to air, in turns. Humphries reports that nearly all the alloys cracked badly along one grain direction. Two tempers, listed as 7075-T73 and 2219-T87, resisted that cracking. Plain protective coatings failed, but coatings plus a zinc chromate primer helped a great deal. Rocket builders needed such warnings.
nasa-tm-19630013938-studies-on-ablation-:
Ernst W. Adams, John D. Warmbrod, and Benton K. Berry of Marshall wrote this study on June 19, 1963. It reviews theory work on ablation heat shields. Ablation protects objects that cross an atmosphere at high speed. The shield chars and sheds material, carrying heat away with it.

The authors came from Marshall's Aeroballistics Division. Their review rests on numerical solutions worked out by computer. Catalog notes say both Earth and Mars entries were treated. A Mars craft meets a thin, strange atmosphere, unlike Earth's. Pulling the theory together in one review helped shield designers plan for planets beyond our own.
nasa-tm-19640018168-an-experimental-stud:
Robert W. Graham, Robert C. Hendricks, and Robert C. Ehlers of Lewis wrote this study. It was prepared for a cryogenic engineering meeting in August 1964. Their subject is heating liquid hydrogen in a pool. Liquid hydrogen is a key rocket fuel, stored near absolute zero.

The team varied pressure across low and very high ranges. They also varied acceleration, to mimic tanks in flight and on the ground. Pool heating drives boiling on the tank's warm surfaces. How bubbles form and break away sets how fast heat moves. Knowing that behavior helped engineers design hydrogen tanks that would not overheat, vent badly, or starve an engine.
nasa-tm-19650012585-the-motion-of-gaseou:
Su-Shu Huang, of Goddard and Catholic University of America, studied how gas streams move in a close binary star system. In such a system, two stars orbit each other closely. Gas can flow between them and around them. Huang asks what rules govern that flow when particles collide.

He first examines a statistical property of the constants that describe particle motion. He then shows that the rate of change of angular momentum does not depend on speed. Those results lead to formulas for the gaseous flow. The work is theory, aimed at explaining real pairs of stars that exchange gas.
nasa-tm-19650070881-studies-of-pilot-con:
C H Woodling of Langley and Carl C Clark of the Naval Air Development Center presented this study in New York in January 1959. Pilots practiced control of space vehicles during launch and reentry on a human centrifuge. A centrifuge spins its rider to copy the forces of flight. Woodling notes that pilot-controlled simulators had become a necessity as aircraft grew more complex.

Real flight was too risky for first tries at such tasks. The centrifuge let pilots feel real forces while staying on the ground. Their performance showed whether a person could still control a vehicle under launch and reentry loads. That question stood at the center of the coming crewed space program.
nasa-tm-19650076351-on-the-use-of-dynami:
Perry W Hanson and George W Jones Jr at Langley explained, in a September 1963 symposium paper, how scaled dynamic models help study two hard loads. Transonic buffet shakes a vehicle in flight. Ground winds bend a tall rocket standing on its pad. Both forces are random and complex, which makes pure calculation difficult, the authors say.

Their answer is the aeroelastic model, scaled to bend like the real vehicle. Tested in wind, such a model reveals response that formulas miss. A two-percent Saturn model appears among their examples. The paper shows model testing at its most practical, aimed at loads that could shake a launch vehicle apart.
nasa-tm-19660020099-a-simulator-study-of:
Lindsay J Lina and Martin T Moul at Langley studied a dangerous stall in a fixed-base simulator, in a paper given in Los Angeles in November 1965. Aircraft with a T-tail, the tailplane set atop the fin, can fall into a deep stall. There, the wing's wake blankets the tail and the nose will not drop. Jet fighters with high tails had long shown pitch-up faults, the authors note.

Newer T-tail transports with rear engines raised the same fear. A simulator lets pilots meet the trap safely and practice recovery. Lina and Moul examine how the aircraft behaves in that state. Their study served a design question with several fatal accidents behind it in that era.
nasa-tm-19670005827-ionospheric-polar-bl:
Yukio Hakura, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this August 1966 paper with Yugoro Takenoshita and Koichi Matsuoka. The co-authors came from the Hiraiso Branch of Japan's Radio Research Laboratories. It builds daily measures of ionospheric blackouts, events where the upper atmosphere absorbs radio signals. Coverage spans the polar cap and the auroral zone, for 1957 through 1965.

Each daily index runs from 0 to 9 and grows roughly with the logarithm of the day's total blackout hours. The auroral zone index generally rose and fell with polar geomagnetic activity. The polar cap index instead tracks activity caused by solar cosmic rays entering the cap, and its yearly average moved with sunspot numbers. The auroral index also showed a clear 27-day repeating pattern, pointing to control by the solar wind.
nasa-tm-19670022994-search-for-the-gamma:
William K. Roberts and David C. Liu, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this report in August 1967. It describes a search for a rare process predicted by quantum electrodynamics. In that process, a photon interacts with a nucleus's electric field and two photons come out. Seeing it would test the theory's picture of the vacuum itself.

The experiment fired gamma rays at lead and copper targets. Detectors sat where the two secondary photons should emerge at right angles to each other, and an energy-summing coincidence technique picked out true pairs. No signal rose above background, so the team set upper limits on the process's cross section for both metals. Those limits sat far above the theoretical predictions, so the theory escaped a rigorous test. Still, the authors argue, the experience shows the predicted range is reachable with improved technique, and they discuss the needed improvements.
nasa-tm-19680012452-modulo-acquisition-o:
Solomon Levine, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1968. It treats modulo acquisition of ambiguity resolving tracking codes, the signals ground stations use to measure a spacecraft's range. Before any ranging can happen, the station must lock onto the incoming code at exactly the right repeating point.

With sidetone ranging, Levine explains, phase locked loops make acquisition easy. A pure pseudo-random code system is slower: the local copy must be shifted bit by bit against the received code until the two correlate. A hybrid system using both can exploit the sidetone's ambiguous range reading to acquire the pseudo-random code automatically and rapidly. Compared with the code-only approach, this modulo technique cuts acquisition time to a small fraction, raises the detection threshold, and considerably reduces encoder complexity.
nasa-tm-19680013859-human-information-pr:
T. E. Wempe and D. L. Baty of NASA's Ames Research Center measured how fast people handle information while tracking in this 1968 study. Subjects flew one-axis and two-axis tracking tasks while also doing a second listening task. The work asks how much a person can take in before performance hits a clear limit.

Adding a second tracking channel or the listening task lowered the rate on each channel. Apart from that drop, the channels acted like parallel paths that add together. Total rate still stopped at a limit tied to the order of the system being controlled. The results help predict pilot workload on complex aerospace missions with many tasks at once.
nasa-tm-19680016283-on-the-dynamics-of-a:
Joseph A. Burns and Gerald Halpern of Goddard Space Flight Center study charged particle motion in a spiral magnetic field in this May 1968 preprint. The spiral field is an ideal model of the interplanetary magnetic field. Energetic particles follow a guiding center path as they drift through that field.

The authors present formulas for every part of the drift velocity. Comparing the parts shows the electric drift is by far the largest for cases of physical interest. They then derive a fuller expression using only that dominant drift. The results help scientists track how energetic particles move through interplanetary space between the Sun and Earth.
nasa-tm-19680019214-a-study-of-refrigera:
Jesse P. Blalock of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston studied a cold-based first aid treatment for pit viper snakebite in this June 1968 memorandum. The method pairs refrigeration with a constricting band on the bitten limb. Blalock asked whether it could replace the standard incision and suction procedure.

A literature search showed experts already doubted incision and suction, citing limits and possible harm. Blalock injected rabbits with eastern diamondback rattlesnake venom. Treated animals were then compared with untreated animals for survival time. The treated group showed a significant increase in survival time. Blalock closes with recommendations for first aid procedures based on the study.
nasa-tm-19680020381-pressure-induced-mic:
W. Ho and I. A. Kaufman, linked to North American Rockwell and Columbia University's Radiation Laboratory, studied how nitrogen gas absorbs microwaves under pressure. Nitrogen on its own should pass microwaves freely, yet squeezed gas absorbs some of the signal. Their report measures that pressure-induced absorption at one microwave frequency, across wide ranges of heat and pressure.

All readings were taken at a single frequency while pressure rose to well over a hundred times normal air pressure. The authors express the loss in a compact formula tied to gas density and temperature. Combining their result with earlier far-infrared work, they then calculate a lasting property of the nitrogen molecule, its quadrupole moment.
nasa-tm-19680027714-radiative-transfer-b:
James E. Hansen of the Institute for Space Studies at Goddard Space Flight Center develops a faster way to compute radiative transfer in this paper. The problem is diffuse reflection of light from a plane parallel atmosphere. Exact solutions exist only for very simple scattering patterns, so practical cases need numerical work.

Hansen builds on a doubling principle first used by van de Hulst. Start with a layer so thin that its scattering follows directly from the phase function. Then double the layer repeatedly to reach full atmospheric thickness. The method skips solving the full transfer equation numerically. Hansen applies it to spectral scattering by clouds in the near-infrared. There the phase function peaks strongly in the forward direction.
nasa-tm-19690018532-a-note-on-the-plasma:
J. M. Grebowsky wrote this March 1969 preprint, numbered X-621-69-42, on the plasma moment equations in a dipole field. A dipole field, like a bar magnet's, models the magnetism of Earth and other planets. Plasma trapped in such a field follows its curved lines, which makes the motion equations awkward in ordinary coordinates.

Grebowsky sets up a coordinate system fitted to the field itself. One direction runs along the field, one circles around it, and one follows the dipole's equipotential lines. He then rewrites the speed terms of the continuity and momentum equations in those directions. The short note gives plasma theorists a cleaner frame for studying distributions and waves in planetary fields.
nasa-tm-19690020177-effects-of-thermal-s:
John J. Smithrick of Lewis Research Center thermal-shock tested thin-film cadmium sulfide solar cells in this report. Cells on Kapton, copper, and molybdenum substrates were heated, then dipped into liquid nitrogen. The cycles ran in an inert atmosphere, with heating held at a set warm temperature.

Kapton substrate cells split in the cadmium sulfide layer and delaminated. Their voltage and fill factor held steady, while current and power fell in proportion to lost area. nasa-tm-19700024989-the-effects-of-wind-:

nasa-tm-19700025191-csm-fuel-requirement:

nasa-tm-19700026507-development-of-a-spa:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note, number MSC-67-EE-12. It reports the development of an atomic timing system for spacecraft. nasa-tm-19700027853-orbital-reconnaissan:
Richard N. Green and Sue W. Souders of the Langley Research Center in Virginia wrote this report for Project Viking. It presents a computer program for planning orbital reconnaissance of Mars. Viking orbiters would photograph the planet to pick landing sites.

nasa-tm-19710007936-dynamic-data-analysi:
Robert C. Ward of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It explains the dynamic data analysis techniques inside Langley's time series computer program. The program studies records that vary with time, such as vibration data from flight tests.

nasa-tm-19710023840-energy-exchanges-dur:

pico-oratio-de-hominis-dignitate-latin:

pomponazzi-de-incantationibus-1556-latin:

ranke-history-popes-vol-2-austin:

ranke-history-popes-vol-3-austin:

remy-daemonolatreiae-1595-latin:

reuchlin-de-arte-cabalistica-1517-latin:
Johannes Reuchlin, a German lawyer and scholar of Hebrew, published De arte cabalistica at Hagenau in 1517. The Latin work, in three books, is the founding text of Christian Kabbalah. It mixes Hebrew and Greek passages into a staged debate among three speakers.

rituale-romanum-latin:

secretum-secretorum-1501-latin:
The Secretum Secretorum, the Secret of Secrets, pretends to be Aristotle's private counsel to his pupil Alexander. This Latin edition was printed at Bologna in 1501. The medieval work is a mirror for princes, a guide to ruling, with health lore, physiognomy, and talismanic matter worked through it.

The magical streak sets it apart from plainer mirrors of rule. Few medieval books traveled so far in so many tongues. The 1501 printing shows the text still current at the dawn of the press age.
sinistrari-demoniality-1879-english-lati:
Ludovico Maria Sinistrari was a Franciscan friar and demon expert in late 1600s Italy. His Latin treatise on demoniality stayed in manuscript until it was found in 1872. The first English version came out at Paris in 1879, printed side by side with the Latin.

Sinistrari argues that incubi and succubi, the night demons of old lore, are real bodily beings with minds of their own. He asks how the law and the Church should judge acts tied to them. The odd, careful book is a late high point of Catholic demon thought.
spee-cautio-criminalis-1631-latin:
Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women condemned as witches. His Cautio Criminalis, printed at Rinteln in 1631, attacks the witch trials from inside the system. The Latin text is that of the first edition.

Spee lays out 51 doubts about how the trials worked. He shows how torture forced false claims, how one claim led to the next arrest, and why no accused person could ever prove innocence. The book helped turn opinion in Germany against the burnings. It remains one of the bravest books of the witch-trial age.
the-american-republic-its-constitution-t: Orestes Brownson's 1865 work on the American republic: its Constitution, tendencies, and destiny, written during the Civil War. the-glittering-plain:

the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-daisy-cha: The Trial, or More Links of the Daisy Chain, by Charlotte Yonge. The May family continues. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsies-of: George Borrow's 1841 classic, part travel memoir and part ethnography, about the Roma people of Spain. trithemius-polygraphia-1518-latin:

trithemius-steganographia-latin:
